sequences.title: La Famille: Meet the Family (and the Cats)

screens.title: Family words are your first French superpower
lines: When you introduce your family in French, every person wears a tiny gender tag: LA mère (the mother) but LE père (the father).
Spot the tag and whole sentences fall into place — it even works for the cats.

screens.framing: No grade, just explore — French drops clues everywhere. What would YOU guess?

screens.title: Point at anything and ask
lines: In a French classroom you can survive with ONE question: « Qu'est-ce que c'est ? » — 'What is it?'
The answer is always « C'est… » plus the object — and every object wears un or une, its gender badge.

screens.framing: Zero pressure — just listen to the sounds and take a swing. Guessing is how detectives warm up.

screens.title: Colors that change their outfit
lines: Amal's yarn stash speaks French today: la laine bleue, la laine verte… and the color word itself changes its spelling!
French adjectives AGREE with their noun — and they line up AFTER it: un pull bleu, never un bleu pull.

screens.framing: No grade here — sniff out the cognate hiding in the question and take your best shot.

items.prompt: Sofia slides a photo across the desk: « Voici ma famille ! » What is she showing Amal?
items.hint: « Famille » looks a LOT like an English word…
items.explanation: « Voici ma famille » = 'Here is my family.' French and English share heaps of look-alike words — trust the clues.

items.prompt: Let's decode 'my': why is it « ma mère » but « mon oncle »? Walk through it.

steps.text: Every French noun wears a gender tag: la mère (mother) and la tante (aunt) are feminine; le père (father) and l'oncle (uncle) are masculine.
'My' copies the tag: MA for feminine (ma mère, ma tante), MON for masculine (mon père, mon oncle).

check.question: La sœur (the sister) is feminine — so 'my sister' is…

steps.text: More than one? MES covers every plural, no matter the gender: mes parents (my parents), mes chats (my cats).
That's the whole machine: ma + feminine, mon + masculine, mes + plural. Family unlocked.

items.prompt: Finish Amal's introduction — match each 'my' to the noun's gender tag.
items.hint: Feminine takes ma, masculine takes mon, any plural takes mes.
items.explanation: Ma mère (feminine), mon oncle (masculine), mes parents (plural) — the tag does the choosing for you.

items.prompt: What does « la mère » mean?
items.hint: Think of the English word 'maternal'.
items.explanation: La mère = the mother — English 'maternal' hides the same Latin root.

items.prompt: Match each family word to its English.
items.hint: The « grand- » words are one generation up.
items.explanation: Frère and sœur are the siblings; grand-mère and grand-père are the grandparents.

items.prompt: Amal writes her first French sentence: « J'ai un chat. » What did she say?
items.hint: « J'ai » comes from avoir — 'to have'.
items.explanation: J'ai = 'I have', so j'ai un chat = 'I have a cat.' (Only one? She'd better learn deux chats fast.)

items.prompt: Tap play. Which family member do you hear?
items.hint: No sound? It sounds like: mah MAIR.
items.explanation: « Ma mère » = my mother — that long 'air' sound is the giveaway.

items.prompt: « Les parents » means…
items.hint: It's the most look-alike word on the whole list.
items.explanation: Les parents = the parents: la mère + le père. (In France it can also mean 'relatives' — sneaky bonus fact.)

items.prompt: Type the French for 'the brother' — include le or la.
items.hint: Brothers are masculine, so it's le. The word rhymes with « mère ».
items.explanation: Le frère = the brother. The little accent (è) marks that open 'eh' sound.

items.prompt: Tap play. What is this proud cat-owner announcing?
items.hint: No sound? It's like: zhay duh SHAH.
items.explanation: J'ai deux chats = 'I have two cats.' The final -ts goes silent — French cats are stealthy.

items.prompt: Finish the family introductions — 'my' must match each noun's gender.

lines: Here is my aunt. → Voici [[ma]] tante.
And here is my uncle. → Et voici [[mon]] oncle.

items.hint: La tante is feminine; l'oncle is masculine.
items.explanation: Ma tante but mon oncle — the gender tag picks your 'my' every single time.

items.prompt: Sort each family member by gender tag: would you say MON or MA?
items.hint: Cousine with the extra -e is the girl cousin.
items.explanation: Masculine words take mon, feminine words take ma — and the -e on cousine marks her as feminine.

items.prompt: Build the sentence: 'I have a brother and a sister.'
items.hint: Start with 'I have', then list the siblings.
items.explanation: J'ai un frère et une sœur — notice un for the brother but une for the sister.

items.prompt: Tap play. What is this person telling you?
items.hint: No sound? It's like: zhuh nay pah duh shee-EN.
items.explanation: Ne… pas wraps the verb like a sandwich: je N'ai PAS de chien = I do NOT have a dog.

items.prompt: Amal wants to say 'I don't have a sister.' Which sentence is correct?
options: Je ne pas ai de sœur.
items.hint: Two rules: ne…pas hugs the verb, and after pas, un/une shrinks to de.
items.explanation: Ne…pas wraps around ai, and un/une becomes de in the negative: je n'ai pas DE sœur.

items.prompt: Match each form of avoir (to have) to its English.
items.hint: Avoir is the family verb — everyone HAS somebody.
items.explanation: J'ai, tu as, elle a, nous avons — four faces of avoir you'll use constantly.

items.prompt: Complete each sentence with the right form of avoir: as, a, or avons.
items.hint: Tu and il forms SOUND identical — only the spelling changes. Nous gets the long one.
items.explanation: Tu as, il a, nous avons — tiny words doing big family business.

items.prompt: Tap play. What does this person say about their family?
items.hint: No sound? It's like: noo zah-VON oon grond fah-MEE.
items.explanation: Nous avons = we have; une grande famille = a big family. The s of nous links into avons: 'noo-Zavons'.

items.prompt: Amal introduces her two cats in French. Type the missing word: « J'ai deux ___ . »
items.hint: Two cats means plural — give chat its silent costume letter.
items.explanation: J'ai deux chats — the plural -s is written but never pronounced.

items.prompt: One word in this introduction is wrong. Tap it.
items.hint: Check the gender tag on frère.
items.explanation: Frère is masculine, so it needs MON: voici mon frère Paul.

items.prompt: Tap play. Who has which pet?
items.answer: My cousin (a girl) has a dog
options: My cousin (a girl) has a dog
My cousin (a boy) has a dog
items.hint: No sound? It's like: mah koo-ZEEN ah uh shee-EN. Listen for the 'een' ending.
items.explanation: Cousine with the 'een' sound is the girl cousin — cousin (a boy) ends in a nasal 'an' sound instead.

items.prompt: Build the sentence: 'She does not have a cat.'
items.hint: The ne…pas sandwich: n' goes before the verb, pas right after it.
items.explanation: Elle n'a pas de chat — tragic, but grammatically perfect.

items.prompt: Two of these statements about French family words are true. Tap the lie.

truths: « La fille » can mean 'the daughter' or 'the girl'.

items.hint: One of these words got matched with the wrong relatives.
items.explanation: Mes parents = my parents (mother and father). Fils and fille really are the son and the daughter.

items.prompt: Caption challenge for the photo wall (right under the K-pop posters): write 'I have a brother and two cats.' in French.
answer: J'ai un frère et deux chats
Jai un frère et deux chats
items.hint: Start with j'ai; the brother takes un, and the cats need their plural -s.
items.explanation: J'ai un frère et deux chats — counting, articles, and plurals in one caption. Très pro.

items.prompt: A French classmate taps Amal's desk and asks: « Qu'est-ce que c'est ? » What do they want to know?
items.hint: It's THE pointing-at-things question — four words mashed into one sound: kess-kuh-SAY.
items.explanation: Qu'est-ce que c'est ? = 'What is it?' You'll ask it a hundred times, and that's exactly the point.

items.prompt: How do you ANSWER « Qu'est-ce que c'est ? » Let's build the reply — and pick the right un or une.

steps.text: The answer formula is C'est… ('it is'): Qu'est-ce que c'est ? → C'est un livre. (It's a book.)
Un or une? Masculine objects take UN (un stylo, un cahier); feminine objects take UNE (une règle, une trousse).

check.question: La chaise (the chair) is feminine. 'It's a chair' is…

steps.text: Several things? DES does plural duty: des stylos = some pens. And to say what's THERE, use il y a: Il y a des livres. (There are books.)

check.question: « Il y a un ordinateur » means…

steps.text: So: c'est NAMES one thing, il y a announces what EXISTS somewhere. Two power tools, one backpack.

items.prompt: Answer the classmate — fill in un or une. (Cahier is masculine; trousse is feminine.)
items.hint: Masculine → un, feminine → une.
items.explanation: Un cahier, une trousse — the badge matches the noun, not the speaker.

items.prompt: What does « un livre » mean?
items.hint: Think of a 'library'.
items.explanation: Un livre = a book — same root as 'library'. (Un cahier is the notebook.)

items.prompt: Pack the pencil case: match each object to its English.
items.hint: Crayon is a French trap — it's NOT the waxy kind.
items.explanation: Stylo = pen, crayon = pencil (sneaky!), règle = ruler, cahier = notebook.

items.prompt: The mascot points at itself and purrs: « Qu'est-ce que c'est ?… C'est un chat ! » What did it say?
items.hint: You met « chat » back in the Family region.
items.explanation: C'est un chat = it's a cat. The mascot enjoys asking itself easy questions.

items.prompt: Tap play. Which school object do you hear?
items.hint: No sound? It's like: uh stee-LOH.
items.explanation: Un stylo = a pen. Crayon would have given you that 'cray' sound instead.

items.prompt: On a French class schedule, « le français » is which subject?
items.hint: The most famous cognate of them all.
items.explanation: Le français = French class. L'anglais = English and l'histoire = history — schedules are cognate gold.

items.prompt: Type the French for 'a pencil' (with un or une) — the one Amal sketches K-pop fan art with.
items.hint: It's the false friend from the matching game — and it's masculine.
items.explanation: Un crayon = a pencil. In France, a wax crayon needs its full name: un crayon de cire.

items.prompt: Tap play. How does this student feel about math?
items.hint: No sound? It's like: zhem lay MAT.
items.explanation: J'aime les maths = I like math. Excellent taste.

items.prompt: Gender-badge sort: does each classroom object take UN or UNE?
items.hint: Exactly three of these are feminine — the rest wear un.
items.explanation: Un livre, un crayon, un bureau, un ordinateur — but une règle, une trousse, une chaise. Badges must be memorized, alas.

items.prompt: Match each school subject to its English.
items.hint: Several of these are nearly free — cognates!
items.explanation: Subjects come with le/la/les attached: les maths, les sciences, l'histoire, l'anglais, le français.

items.prompt: Build the sentence: 'In my room, there are three K-pop posters.'
items.hint: Start with the place, then drop in the magic phrase « il y a ».
items.explanation: Il y a = 'there is' AND 'there are' — one phrase covers both. Dans ma chambre, il y a trois posters de K-pop.

items.prompt: Tap play. What is the surprising classroom news?
items.answer: There are two cats in the classroom
options: There are two cats in the classroom
There are two desks in the classroom
There is a cat on the chair

data.audioText: Il y a deux chats dans la classe !

items.hint: No sound? It's like: eel-ee-AH duh SHAH dahn lah KLASS.
items.explanation: Il y a deux chats dans la classe — there are two cats in class. Best school day ever.

items.prompt: Fill in the French for 'the': le, la, or les.
items.hint: Masculine → le, feminine → la, any plural → les.
items.explanation: Le livre, la chaise, les stylos — 'the' owns three French outfits.

items.prompt: Amal announces: « J'aime le français, mais je n'aime pas l'histoire. » What did she say?
items.answer: She likes French but not history
options: She likes French but not history
She likes history but not French
items.hint: « Mais » = but, and the ne…pas sandwich flips the second verb.
items.explanation: J'aime = I like; je n'aime pas = I don't like. Mais (but) pivots between them.

items.prompt: Tap play. Which object is being identified?
items.hint: No sound? It's like: say toon REGL.
items.explanation: C'est une règle = it's a ruler. Fun fact: règle also means 'rule' — rulers enforce straight lines.

items.prompt: Amal's big line in the school play: « Je ___ une star de K-pop ! » (I AM a K-pop star!) Type the missing word.
items.hint: It's from être (to be): je …, tu es, c'est.
items.explanation: Je suis = I am. Être's forms barely resemble each other — even French kids side-eye that verb.

items.prompt: Bake-sale poster supplies! Finish each line with un, une, or des.

lines: a chair for the cookie table → [[une]] chaise

items.hint: One masculine thing → un, one feminine thing → une, several of anything → des.
items.explanation: Un stylo, des stylos, une chaise — des is the plural badge meaning 'some'.

items.prompt: One chunk of this backpack report is wrong. Tap it.
items.hint: Check the gender badge on the book.
items.explanation: Livre (book) is masculine: UN livre. « Une livre » actually means 'a pound' — a backpack full of weight, not words!

items.prompt: Tap play. Which object does the speaker name?

data.audioText: Qu'est-ce que c'est ? C'est un sac à dos.

items.hint: No sound? The answer sounds like: sak-ah-DOH.
items.explanation: C'est un sac à dos = it's a backpack — literally a 'bag for the back'.

items.prompt: Build the sentence: 'I don't like history.'
items.hint: Same ne…pas sandwich you used with avoir — now hugging aime.
items.explanation: Je n'aime pas l'histoire — the negation sandwich works on every verb in French.

items.prompt: Two of these classroom-French facts are true. Tap the lie.

truths: « Des » means 'some' — used for more than one thing.
data.lie: « Une » goes with masculine nouns like livre and stylo.

items.hint: Check which badge livre and stylo actually wear.
items.explanation: Livre and stylo are masculine, so they take UN — une belongs to feminine nouns like règle and trousse.

items.prompt: Desk-tour challenge: write in French 'On my desk, there is a computer and a K-pop poster.'
answer: Sur mon bureau, il y a un ordinateur et un poster de K-pop
Sur mon bureau il y a un ordinateur et un poster de K-pop
Sur mon bureau, il y a un ordinateur et un poster de K pop
Sur mon bureau il y a un ordinateur et un poster de K pop
items.hint: Start with « Sur mon bureau », then il y a, then list both objects with un.
items.explanation: Sur mon bureau, il y a un ordinateur et un poster de K-pop. Il y a handles 'there is' AND 'there are' — one phrase, zero stress.

items.prompt: At the yarn shop, the owner holds up a skein and asks Amal: « De quelle couleur est cette laine ? » What does she want to know?
options: How much does this yarn cost?
items.hint: « Couleur » is hiding in plain sight.
items.explanation: De quelle couleur est… ? = 'What color is… ?' — your go-to question in any yarn or art shop.

items.prompt: Watch one color change its outfit: un chat noir → une chatte noire → des chats noirs.

steps.text: Color words come AFTER the noun in French: un chat noir = a black cat (literally 'a cat black').
Feminine noun? The color grows an -e: une chatte noire (a black girl-cat). With vert you can even HEAR it: un pull vert ('vair') → une robe verte ('vairt').

check.question: La trousse is feminine. 'A green pencil case' is…

steps.text: Plural adds -s: des chats noirs. Feminine plural gets both: des chattes noires. (The -s stays silent — sneaky.)
Already ends in -e, like rouge or jaune? It never changes: un pull rouge, une robe rouge. And orange + marron refuse ALL changes — invariable rebels.

items.prompt: Label Amal's yarn-basket chart — make each color agree.
items.hint: Écharpe (scarf) and pelote (yarn ball) are both feminine.
items.explanation: Une écharpe verte, des pelotes vertes — the adjective copies gender AND number from its noun.

items.prompt: Amal's favorite skein is labeled « rouge ». What color is it?
items.hint: Think of 'rouge' blush makeup.
items.explanation: Rouge = red — same word as the red blush. Bonus: it never changes form, since it already ends in -e.

items.prompt: Match each color to its English.
items.hint: Two of them are near-twins of the English.
items.explanation: Bleu, vert, jaune, noir, blanc — the core palette. Mont Blanc literally means 'White Mountain'!

items.prompt: « Un chat noir » crosses your path. What is it?
items.hint: Noir like 'film noir' — those moody dark movies.
items.explanation: Un chat noir = a black cat. In France plenty of people call it good luck — depends whom you ask!

items.prompt: Tap play. Which color do you hear?
items.hint: No sound? It's like: ZHOHN.
items.explanation: Jaune = yellow — the French j sounds like the s in 'treasure'.

items.prompt: « De quelle couleur est le ciel ? » (What color is the sky?) Answer in French — on a sunny day.
items.hint: It's almost the same word in English.
items.explanation: Le ciel est bleu — the sky is blue. (Marron is brown and rose is pink.)

items.prompt: Type the French for 'green'.
items.hint: Think 'verdant' — a fancy English word for green and leafy.
items.explanation: Vert = green (verte with feminine nouns). Verdant fields, champs verts.

items.prompt: Tap play. What does Amal say about her new yarn?
items.hint: No sound? It's like: lah LEN ay ROHZ.
items.explanation: La laine est rose = the yarn is pink. Rose the color, rose the flower — same word.

items.prompt: Agreement sort: which color forms describe UN PULL (masculine) and which describe UNE ROBE (feminine)?
items.hint: The extra -e is the feminine signature.
items.explanation: Un pull bleu/vert/noir/gris, but une robe bleue/verte/noire/grise — the -e tags along with feminine nouns.

items.prompt: Match each masculine color to its feminine form.
items.hint: Two of them do more than just add an -e.
items.explanation: Blanc → blanche and violet → violette are shape-shifters; vert and gris simply add -e.

items.prompt: Build the sentence — Amal shows off a sweater she knit: 'I have a blue sweater.'
items.hint: In French, the color goes AFTER the sweater.
items.explanation: J'ai un pull bleu — adjective after the noun. « Un bleu pull » would make French knitters wince.

items.prompt: Tap play. What is this student showing you?
items.hint: No sound? It's like: zhay oon trooss vee-oh-LET.
items.explanation: Une trousse violette = a purple pencil case — violet doubles its t before the feminine -e.

items.prompt: Two cats, one color, two spellings. Fill in gris or grise.
items.hint: Feminine nouns pull an extra -e onto the color.
items.explanation: Le chat est gris, la chatte est grise — and you can hear this one: 'gree' vs 'greez'.

items.prompt: Amal knits orange socks. « Les chaussettes » is feminine plural — which is correct?
items.hint: Orange is one of the two rebel colors.
items.explanation: Orange (like marron) is invariable — it never takes -e or -s. Des chaussettes orange, des pulls marron.

items.prompt: Tap play. What color is the speaker's backpack?

data.audioText: De quelle couleur est ton sac à dos ? Il est noir.

items.hint: No sound? The answer sounds like: NWAHR.
items.explanation: Il est noir = it's black. Noir as in 'film noir' — moody black-and-white movies.

items.prompt: Describe the bakery window — finish each line with the right form of blanc.
items.hint: Blanc is a shape-shifter: its feminine form rhymes with 'avalanche'.
items.explanation: Un gâteau blanc, de la farine blanche — blanc → blanche is one of the two big shape-shifters.

items.prompt: Amal's new yarn is purple. Complete with the right form: « La laine est ___ . »
items.hint: La laine is feminine — and violet doubles a letter before its -e.
items.explanation: La laine est violette — violet doubles the t before taking the feminine -e.

items.prompt: One chunk of this outfit report is in the wrong order. Tap it.
items.hint: Where do French colors stand — before or after the noun?
items.explanation: Colors follow the noun: un pull bleu. The scarf got it right: une écharpe grise.

items.prompt: Tap play. What is the speaker bragging about?
items.hint: No sound? It's like: may duh SHAH son NWAHR.
items.explanation: Mes deux chats sont noirs — plural cats, plural adjective. The -s on noirs is silent but loyal.

items.prompt: Build the question: 'What color is your pencil case?'
items.hint: The question phrase « De quelle » launches the sentence.
items.explanation: De quelle couleur est ta trousse ? — the color question runs: de quelle couleur + est + the thing.

items.prompt: Two of these color-grammar facts are true. Tap the lie.

truths: « Orange » and « marron » never change — not for feminine, not for plural.
Color words usually come AFTER the noun: un chat gris.
data.lie: To make « rouge » feminine, you add an extra -e: « rougee ».

items.hint: What's the rule for colors that already end in -e?
items.explanation: Rouge already ends in -e, so it never changes: un pull rouge, une robe rouge. No double-e words in this game!

items.prompt: Portrait caption challenge: write in French 'I have a white cat and a black cat.'
answer: J'ai un chat blanc et un chat noir
Jai un chat blanc et un chat noir
items.hint: Both colors go AFTER chat — and chat is masculine, so no extra -e.
items.explanation: J'ai un chat blanc et un chat noir — colors after the noun, masculine forms, zero agreement drama.
